articles.summary: China is looking to “optimize and enhance” its social security program. People fear that will translate to pressure on gig economy workers and rural migrant workers.

articles.title: What the New China-North Korea Bridge Really Means
articles.full_text:
12 years after construction finished, the New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. Will North Korea’s economy open too?
This photo from North Korean state media shows the New Yalu River Bridge between China and North Korea on the day of its official ribbon-cutting ceremony, Oct. 15, 2026.
The New Yalu River Bridge, which links Dandong in China’s Liaoning province with Sinuiju in North Pyongan province, has finally opened, a full 12 years after construction finished in 2014. The two countries held an opening ceremony on October 15 and began running cargo trucks across the bridge, which is known as the Amnok River bridge in North Korea.
For years the bridge symbolized China-North Korea economic cooperation and also the practical limits on how far that cooperation could actually go. Now it is finally doing the job it was built for.
The two countries agreed to build the bridge in 2009, and construction began the following year. It was a major project meant to get past the logistical limits of the existing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge. A four-lane bridge more than 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) long could greatly expand the flow of goods between Dandong and Sinuiju. China was willing to pay for construction to open a new channel for economic cooperation with the North.
Fifteen years ago, I was reporting for Daily NK in China. Back then, Dandong was full of anticipation about the bridge. People everywhere said a new crossing would bring a surge in China-North Korea trade, and that a new economic zone would grow up around Sinuiju and Dandong. Chinese businesspeople expected trade with the North to expand, and property prices near the planned development areas began to climb.
In August 2011, Daily NK reported that work on a pontoon bridge for the construction was 70 percent complete and that nearby real estate prices were rising. Some in Dandong even speculated that the bridge might lead North Korea to open its economy more widely. I still remember that mood clearly from my time on the ground.
Reality fell short of those hopes. The bridge was finished in 2014, but the North Korean side never properly built the connecting roads or customs facilities. Ups and downs in bilateral relations, international sanctions, and the COVID-19 border closure followed, and the bridge stayed shut for years. It was a long wait for the Chinese businesspeople who had hoped for new opportunities, and for everyone who had expected trade with the North to grow.
North Korea’s insularity alone doesn’t explain the delay. The two countries’ economic interests, the political climate, sanctions, and other factors all played a part. What is clear, though, is that North Korean authorities took a long and cautious approach to how much economic contact with the outside world they would allow, and how they would manage it.
In the end, the hard part was not building the bridge. It was getting past the North Korean authorities’ extremely narrow threshold. Pyongyang wanted the economic benefits, but it never let down its guard against the changes outside contact might bring. The 12 years the bridge sat effectively unused lay bare this contradiction at the heart of the North Korean economy.
More Trade Means New Opportunities and New Tests
So now that the bridge is open, will North Korea’s economy change? In the short term, we can expect more trade and more efficient transport between the two countries. Freight that used to pile onto the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge can now be spread out, and there is finally a route that can reliably carry larger volumes of goods.
Still, it would be a mistake to assume the opening will quickly produce a jump in trade or better lives for ordinary North Koreans. How much actually moves will depend on customs procedures, transport costs, trade permits, and how goods are distributed inside North Korea. A wider bridge does not necessarily mean North Korea’s economy has opened any wider.
The bigger story may be how distribution inside North Korea changes. Markets are still central to how ordinary North Koreans make a living. Lately, however, the authorities have not simply been suppressing the general markets. They have been using state-run stores, state grain shops, and other retail outlets to expand state control over distribution and sales.
Under these conditions, if more imports flow across the bridge, state-approved trading companies and distribution agencies are likely to benefit first. In the past, private merchants brought in imported goods through various channels and supplied them to markets. That model may give way further to one where the state manages the import and allocation of goods, with markets and retail outlets operating beneath it.
Private merchants could still find new openings. More stable logistics and a larger supply of Chinese consumer goods and raw materials could mean more choice for shoppers and steadier prices for some items. If factories and enterprises can source raw materials more easily, production could benefit too.
But if the state tightens its grip on imports and distribution, the gains could concentrate in the agencies that hold trade permits and the power to allocate goods. Private merchants would become more dependent on state-designated distribution channels, and the various costs and informal payments they face could well rise.
How the bridge ties into North Korea’s “20×10” regional development policy is also worth watching. The North is racing to build local industrial factories, but putting up a building is one thing and running a factory is another. What matters is not how many factories have been built. It is how many days a month they actually run, where their raw materials come from, and what prices residents pay for what they produce. Without a steady supply of raw materials, electricity, and production equipment, these factories will struggle to operate.
Here, more Chinese raw materials and supplies could improve operating conditions at some local factories. Yet the more these factories rely on Chinese inputs, the further they drift from the self-reliant local economy the authorities keep promoting. 
Development around Sinuiju also deserves attention. According to a recent Daily NK investigation, North Korea has reportedly pitched Chinese businesspeople on a plan to develop the area behind the bridge and some 40 square kilometers (15 square miles) of southern Sinuiju into an economic hub for logistics, processing, trade, and commerce. This suggests Pyongyang wants to use the bridge’s opening to make more economic use of the border region.
We should still separate development plans from actual investment and production. Current United Nations sanctions sharply restrict imports of industrial equipment, exports of North Korean processed goods, and joint ventures. Early on, the benefits will likely be limited to better customs and logistics, with any large-scale industrial cooperation moving slowly.
Above all, North Korea’s economy could become even more dependent on China. Deeper reliance on Chinese raw materials, consumer goods, capital, and logistics networks might give the economy a short-term lift. It could also leave the economy more exposed to shifts in Chinese policy and trade conditions. The gap between the self-reliance the regime preaches and its real dependence on China could grow wider.
Ultimately, the bridge’s opening is both an opportunity and a major test for North Korea’s economy. The question is what the authorities do with the extra goods and economic openings. Will they let ordinary people expand their economic activity, or will the state tighten its hold on profits and distribution channels? The answer looks set to shape the structure of North Korea’s economy in the years ahead.
The number of trucks crossing the bridge is not the only thing to watch. Actual freight volumes, the goods being traded, customs procedures, and shipping costs all matter. But to really judge how North Korea’s economy is changing, we need to follow where those goods go, who controls the trade, and how it ultimately affects people’s daily lives.
That means tracking specific economic indicators over time. How many trucks cross the bridge each month? How much does the share of Chinese goods in markets change? How are people’s purchases split between state-run outlets and the general markets, and how is that changing?
We also need to look at how many days local factories with more Chinese inputs actually run and how much they produce, and how more imports affect consumer prices and people’s purchasing power.
With these questions in mind, the Daily NK sees a need to keep tracking changes in North Korea’s economic structure and in people’s living conditions. Comparing trends at three months, six months, and one year after the opening should give a clearer picture of how the economy is really changing.
What matters here is the direction of change, not whether a single number rises or falls. If imports go up but purchasing power doesn’t improve, we need to find out why. If state stores see more customers, we need to know whether private market trade is shrinking or whether both are growing. More goods coming in and people finding it easier to buy things are two very different matters.
In particular, comparing economic conditions in major cities such as Sinuiju (North Pyongan province), Pyongsong (South Pyongan province), and Hyesan (Ryanggang province) can show whether more border trade is reaching people inland and in the provinces. Even if imports grow at the border, distribution costs and local supply conditions mean residents in different areas may feel the change very differently.
We also need to see whether development in Sinuiju actually creates jobs and raises incomes. New facilities, roads, and housing are hard to count as a success if residents are hit with demands for money or forced labor mobilizations along the way. Beyond how the development looks, we need to see who bears the costs and who reaps the benefits.
articles.summary: 12 years after construction finished, the New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. Will North Korea's economy open too?

articles.title: A Warm Welcome for US Secretary of State in Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region.
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed the U.S. capital on October 17, bound for Uzbekistan and India, a journalist asked, “With everything going on in the world and with crisis all over, why are you choosing now, at this time, to go to Uzbekistan?” 
Rubio replied that it was the time that worked for the Central Asians. “This is an important relationship,” he added without expounding on that importance.
In response to questions from the Associated Press regarding Rubio’s schedule, the State Department said the secretary’s “responsibility is not to generate a public profile around every challenge; it is to help the president develop and execute a strategy that advances American interests. Some of the most consequential diplomatic work takes place outside the public spotlight.”
The AP’s October 18 article was titled “Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he’s keeping the most pressing matters at a distance.” Rubio is involved in discussions on a blooming array of international crises, from Iran to China, Gaza to Ukraine, both in his role as secretary of state but also as national security adviser. But he’s not the public face of any of those issues, as the AP argued. 
“The Iran, Gaza, and the Russia-Ukraine conflicts each demand serious attention, but they cannot be approached in isolation from the president’s broader national security objectives,” the State Department told the AP, pushing back against the implication that Rubio was avoiding tackling politically risky issues publicly. “The right question is not whether the secretary is visible enough on a particular issue.”
Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region. There is no free press in Samarkand lobbing difficult questions. There are no allies feeling sour about how much Washington has changed. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in particular, have been enthusiastic to endorse Trump administration initiatives, such as the Board of Peace, that traditional U.S. allies have avoided.

That’s why we’re here now.” That’s a common refrain from the Trump administration, but it does not match reality. 
U.S. foreign policy regarding Central Asia over the last decade has been fairly consistent, as epitomized by the 11-year-old C5+1 format that brought Rubio to Samarkand in the first place to meet with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. 
The format was launched in 2015 when then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited all five regional countries in one trip – a feat Rubio promised to repeat last year during celebrations marking the C5+1’s 10th anniversary. The overarching consistency of U.S. policy toward Central Asia does not mean nothing has changed. No longer do U.S. officials mention human rights or press freedom, areas which Central Asia’s autocratic governments score poorly on. And the Trump administration’s transactional style and its focus on business deals resonates with regional states, even as it narrows relations to the economic sphere. 
When Rubio’s trip to Uzbekistan was first announced in a late September press release from the U.S. Embassy in India – the U.S. ambassador to India is Sergio Gor, who also wears the hat of special envoy for South and Central Asian Affairs – it remarked that the secretary would be traveling with “a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies.”
When the trip’s dates were announced in an October 13 press release, the delegation had become “over 200 business leaders.”
In Samarkand, Rubio referred to the commercial delegation as “incredible,” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining.
On October 14, The Diplomat had asked the State Department if it had a list of the participating businesses. That question went unanswered.

He added, however, that “the realities of investing in Central Asia remain the same.” He pointed to “the realities of distance, logistics, financing, finding a good partner. All of those things remain the same, regardless of whether you have 100 companies, 200 companies, or 20 companies.”
The joint statement published on October 19 – titled “C5+1: Historic Partnership, Prosperous Future” – concluded with this: “We envision C5+1 cooperation that continues to deliver regional solutions to global challenges.”

articles.title: South Korea, US Pull Apart as the Alliance Strains
articles.full_text:
Restricted intelligence sharing, an investment spat, and remarks by a U.S. commander point to a widening gap between the allies.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung meets with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Sep. 22, 2026.
South Korea and the United States are in a tug-of-war over the terms of their alliance. Since March the two governments have clashed over intelligence sharing, investment, and military command. The friction is now visible in small and concrete ways.
The dispute began on March 6 when the South’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young named the North Korean city of Kusong as the site of a uranium enrichment facility. Washington treated the remark as a disclosure of classified information and has since partially restricted the imagery intelligence shared with Seoul on North Korea. Chung has said he learned of the facility from open sources. Washington did not accept the explanation. In April, National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac acknowledged that the two governments held different views of the remark.
A second dispute has become entangled with the first. The U.S.-listed e-commerce company Coupang is under investigation in South Korea over a data breach. A July report by the U.S. House Judiciary Committee accused South Korea’s National Intelligence Service of pressuring officials to pursue the company; the NIS called the claim false. In the same April briefing, Wi said the Coupang case concerned a single company. He nonetheless acknowledged that it was affecting security talks and delaying negotiations.
The intelligence service has been affected directly. Washington barred the agency from a June meeting with Japan on North Korean cyber threats and notified Seoul in writing, according to local media reports. The agency called the exclusion a one-time measure. South Korean Ambassador to the U.S. Kang Kyung-hwa also confirmed that visas for two or three agency employees bound for the embassy in Washington had been delayed. The agency attributed the delays to stricter U.S. entry procedures and denied any link to the intelligence dispute. 
Each incident can be explained on its own, but together the impact is mounting on the intelligence relationship. 
Economic pressure has followed a similar course. Seoul hoped that progress on its $350 billion investment pledge under a trade deal with Washington would restart stalled security talks on nuclear-powered submarines and uranium enrichment. However, the specific terms of investment have become a cause of more tension.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on September 30 that South Korea would invest $54 billion in the Alaska liquefied natural gas project. The trade ministry in Seoul said no decision had been made on whether to invest or how much. Trump pressed the point two days later. On October 2, he warned Seoul of higher costs for staying out of the project. He repeated the investment claim on October 14 in a post on Truth Social.
Before the November 3 midterm elections, Trump has been presenting investment pledges from allies as proof that his tariff policy works. Now Seoul is facing pressure to turn a campaign claim into a financial commitment. The link to security talks gives the dispute weight beyond money.
The strain is also jeopardizing a long-held South Korean military goal. The Lee administration aims to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces by 2028. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson – the officer who currently hold wartime OPCON over Korean forces – has cited the first quarter of 2029.
Then, on October 14, Brunson said at a policy forum in Washington that the conditions for the handover had changed. He pointed to recent North Korean missile launches as evidence. He voiced support for the OPCON transfer but opposed rushing it to meet a political deadline. 
South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said the next day that Seoul had already conveyed its concerns to Washington. The Defense Ministry maintained that the agreed conditions for the transfer remain unchanged.
On October 19, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung was asked about Brunson’s comments. Speaking at the presidential Blue House, Lee told reporters that Seoul must regain wartime OPCON quickly. He added that talks with Washington are basically moving toward its return. Lee also argued that the process should be called a recovery rather than a transfer. 
A second remark from Brunson drew sharper criticism in Seoul. The Demilitarized Zone is a buffer strip between the two Koreas, and the Military Demarcation Line runs through its middle. At the same forum, Brunson said that South Korea begins at the southern fence of the DMZ from the perspective of the United Nations Command. He commands the U.S.-led United Nations Command, which manages the zone to uphold the armistice. A command official countered that there was no question about South Korean sovereignty.
Lawmakers of the ruling Democratic Party objected. Kim Byung-joo, a special presidential adviser on defense policy, demanded a retraction and an apology. The constitution defines the territory of South Korea as the Korean Peninsula and its adjacent islands. Even read narrowly, the remark did little to reassure a partner seeking more control over its own defense.
This isn’t the first time Brunson had sparked controversy. In May, he had likened South Korea to a “dagger in the heart of Asia,” implying that the U.S. would use military assets stationed on the peninsula to thwart China’s “ambitions beyond that.” Seoul has conveyed its concerns about Brunson through several channels and reportedly received a sympathetic reply from the U.S. side.
The latest frictions in South Korea-U.S. relations came as North Korea stepped up its weapons tests. On October 15, North Korean state media reported that the country had tested two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles the day before. That followed a launch of tactical ballistic missiles on October 12. 
A land mine explosion wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ on September 21. The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff have determined that North Korea planted the mines.
On October 19, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement that South Korean troops had fired warning shots at North Korean personnel working on border fortifications. She accused South Korean forces of carrying out 2,870 loudspeaker warnings and 201 warning shots between August 1 and October 17. 
Kim added that the North Korean military was considering deploying more tactical strike weapons along the southern border and resuming loudspeaker broadcasts against the South. She also accused the Lee administration of escalating confrontation faster than his conservative predecessor, Yoon Suk-yeol.
On one level, the alliance is still robust. Communication continues between South Korea and the U.S. as usual. But behind the facade of normal interactions, analysts worry that Seoul is increasingly facing steep costs for saying no to U.S. demands. Across intelligence, trade, and military command, Washington is interlinking issues so that Seoul faces restrictions and threats on all fronts. That looks more like a transactional relationship than the “ironclad” alliance the two foreign ministers reaffirmed on September 18. 
A partner that can only follow is not an ally in the full sense of the word.

articles.title: What the Greens Misunderstand About the Ukraine Conflict
articles.full_text:
As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one. As a political position it is self-defeating, too.
At the end of September, the Australian Greens elected David Shoebridge their new leader. Shoebridge had previously been the party’s spokesperson for foreign affairs and defense, and he retained those responsibilities. While he has always been a combative politician, he immediately created controversy by stating it would be the Greens’ policy to oppose providing further military assistance to Ukraine. Extraordinarily, in a meeting with a number of Ukrainian-Australian community groups last week he left a further sour taste by informing them to not “burn any bridges” by criticizing the Greens.
Shoebridge has said that the party is one of “peace and non-violence,” but within this perspective comes a number of often naïve assumptions about international relations and how states manage conflict. It leads to an odd scenario whereby in proclaiming to be advocates of peace and nonviolence the Greens end up supporting belligerents over victims. 
There are some common traits that “pacifist” parties exhibit that are worth analyzing to understand the Greens’ position. 
The first is that they see violence as a self-perpetuating system. War creates a cycle of fear, militarization, and retaliation. The participants become trapped in an escalating security dilemma – each interpreting the other’s actions as a threat. Therefore peace requires breaking this cycle through restraint, negotiation, and disarmament. This may seem rational on the surface, but it doesn’t account for bad faith actors who believe solely in domination and cannot be trusted to honor any negotiated deal. This is the type of state Ukraine is facing with Russia. 
Alongside this, there is a distrust of the distinction between offensive and defensive power. There is a belief that all military power is essentially used for offensive purposes to varying degrees. Based on that assumption, states which arm themselves in defense – or become a part of an alliance system – are creating the conditions for aggressive actions to occur. Yet this assumes that larger states will naturally respect the sovereignty of their smaller neighbors if they are not armed. This, again, is a misunderstanding of Russia, which views weakness, not strength, as an incentive to escalate. 
What pacifists often believe is that nonviolent resistance is an underutilized alternative to military resistance. There have, of course, been instances where nonviolent resistance has proved incredibly effective, in India during British rule, for example. But nonviolent resistance relies on two factors – when an occupying force requires the assistance of the invaded population, and when this force has enough of a moral compass to be able form some empathy for those it has invaded. Russia simply does not believe that Ukraine is a legitimate nation-state. A disarmed Ukraine is a nonexistent Ukraine.
For some pacifists the priority is to stop conflict, even if the resulting settlement leaves the aggressor state with territorial or political gains. A ceasefire can be argued as saving lives. Yet any settlement that rewards aggression may be an encouragement for further aggression. Russia not only sees Ukraine as an illegitimate state, but also Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Georgia, and Moldova. Rewarding Russia for its invasion of Ukraine sends a signal that it can make military gains in these states too.  
The concept of deterrence is built on the assumption that there will always be belligerence in the world and that peace requires demonstrating and communicating clearly through credible military power that this belligerence will not succeed. For parties like the Greens this is a difficult assumption to swallow. Their belief is that peace can be secured through diplomacy and “good vibes” alone. 
The danger within this pacifism is that it becomes an inflexible political doctrine that treats a refusal to use force as a self-perceived moral victory, and overlooks the actual victims of violence. It confuses the insisted innocence of their own actions with the justice of a real world outcome. 
As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one, but as a political position it is self-defeating. Support for military assistance to Ukraine is a popular position in Australia, and many people believe that Australia should be doing more to help.
Support for the Greens themselves has plateaued at around 12 percent of the Australian public. The party’s approach is mostly to cultivate its status within this 12 percent and they seem disinclined to try to speak to anyone else. Therefore, the party’s position on military assistance to Ukraine probably has less to do with Ukraine itself, and was simply devised as a form of internal moral posturing with little comprehension how peace and security are actually achieved.

For some pacifists the priority is to stop conflict, even if the resulting settlement leaves the aggressor state with territorial or political gains. A ceasefire can be argued as saving lives. Yet any settlement that rewards aggression may be an encouragement for further aggression. Russia not only sees Ukraine as an illegitimate state, but also Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Georgia, and Moldova. Rewarding Russia for its invasion of Ukraine sends a signal that it can make military gains in these states too.  
The concept of deterrence is built on the assumption that there will always be belligerence in the world and that peace requires demonstrating and communicating clearly through credible military power that this belligerence will not succeed. For parties like the Greens this is a difficult assumption to swallow. Their belief is that peace can be secured through diplomacy and “good vibes” alone. 
The danger within this pacifism is that it becomes an inflexible political doctrine that treats a refusal to use force as a self-perceived moral victory, and overlooks the actual victims of violence. It confuses the insisted innocence of their own actions with the justice of a real world outcome. 
As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one, but as a political position it is self-defeating. Support for military assistance to Ukraine is a popular position in Australia, and many people believe that Australia should be doing more to help.
Support for the Greens themselves has plateaued at around 12 percent of the Australian public. The party’s approach is mostly to cultivate its status within this 12 percent and they seem disinclined to try to speak to anyone else. Therefore, the party’s position on military assistance to Ukraine probably has less to do with Ukraine itself, and was simply devised as a form of internal moral posturing with little comprehension how peace and security are actually achieved. 
At the end of September, the Australian Greens elected David Shoebridge their new leader. Shoebridge had previously been the party’s spokesperson for foreign affairs and defense, and he retained those responsibilities. While he has always been a combative politician, he immediately created controversy by stating it would be the Greens’ policy to oppose providing further military assistance to Ukraine. Extraordinarily, in a meeting with a number of Ukrainian-Australian community groups last week he left a further sour taste by informing them to not “burn any bridges” by criticizing the Greens.
Shoebridge has said that the party is one of “peace and non-violence,” but within this perspective comes a number of often naïve assumptions about international relations and how states manage conflict. It leads to an odd scenario whereby in proclaiming to be advocates of peace and nonviolence the Greens end up supporting belligerents over victims. 
Grant Wyeth is a Melbourne-based political analyst specializing in Australia and the Pacific, India and Canada.
articles.summary: As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one. As a political position it is self-defeating, too.

articles.title: Ecological Imbalance Is Driving Bear Encounters in Mongolia
articles.full_text:
As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns.
In recent months, Mongolia has experienced rare bear sightings in its northern provinces. Local authorities have so far been successful in capturing the bears alive and placing the animals back into their natural habitat. The sudden movement of such a large number of bears indicates a deeper ecological imbalance not only in Mongolia but also Russia and Japan. 
As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns. Solo bears, bears with cubs, and lost cubs have been sighted. More alarmingly, bears have encountered nomadic herders, killing one person and injuring several others. People from remote towns and herding communities have reported attacks on livestock. Most of these bears encounters have been reported in Khuvgsul, Bulgan, Darkhan-Uul, and Tuv provinces – all Mongolia’s northern provinces with robust habitat for bears, wolves, elk, deer, and wild boars.   
The sudden surge and the possible migration of bears clearly demonstrate the changing environment in their natural habitat. Khuvsgul, Bulgan, and Darkhan Uul provinces are 51 percent forest and considered a perfect habitat for bears. Mongolia’s boreal forests, known as taiga, offer cedar and pine nuts, types of berries, and water access for bears. In the fall, particularly in the months of August, September, and October, bears forage throughout the taiga with their cubs in preparation for hibernation. 
The increased movement of these bear populations points to several issues in Mongolia’s ecological system. One of the speculated causes is a shortage of food. Mongolia’s extreme weather fluctuations, including shorter summers with amplified heatwaves, can impact vegetation and dry out grasslands. Particularly in Khuvsgul and Bulgan, given the short summer, there is a risk of shortage of berries and nuts. 
In addition, Khuvsgul and Selenge provinces hold one of Mongolia’s critical river basins, which is crucial to the forestry and its natural habitat. One of the remaining questions concerning bear movements is whether these river basins and other water sources are experiencing a fish shortage, caused by climate change and mining activities. 
Given the pristine nature of Northern Mongolia, these provinces are subject to strict environmental scrutiny and protection. Still, mining does occur. Bulgan Province, in particular, is known for its extractive industries, including gold and polymetallic mining (although in comparison to other notable extractive sites, the scale of mining in Bulgan is relatively moderate). 
According to the World Resources Institute, Mongolia’s gold rush has become one of the leading sources of water contamination. Gold extraction sites particularly are a major issue for the local environment. “Lead, arsenic and other toxic chemicals released during gold extraction processes have leached into Mongolia’s groundwater and flowed untreated into rivers,” the WRI found. 
Thus Mongolia’s bear sightings may be related to the country’s mining activities, along with extreme weather aggravated by climate change-caused food shortages. In response, the government and conservation groups are taking a humane approach. Local authorities and the population continue to capture bears and place them back into the wild. 
In comparison, Russia and Japan, both experiencing a similar bear issue, are handling it very differently.   
In Russia’s Far East, in the Siberian forests, the bear population thrives. This October, local authorities in Siberia (Krasnoyarsk), Tuva, and Buryatia reported a surge of bears entering local towns and villages. In Buryatia, the local authority has deployed 24 specialized teams to kill bears. With Russian authorities allowing an “open season,” bear killings will likely increase. 
In 2025, the Environmental Ministry of Japan reported a historic surge in bear sightings and attacks, during which more than 14,600 bears were killed. The ministry believed that “climate change and poor tree-nut harvests have reduced natural food supplies in the mountains.” The ministry also highlighted that around 12,000 brown bears in Hokkaido and Asiatic black bears elsewhere have expanded their roaming range.

Mongolia emphasizes strict legal protections and non-lethal management whereas Russia and Japan both have implemented aggressive population control methods.

Once they associate people with food – in the form of garbage, livestock, gardens, birdfeeders, etc. – they will continue to seek out human settlements. 
In Mongolia’s case specifically, she added, “I wonder too whether some of the increase in sightings and conflict is due to population shifts, in both people and the bears. Paradoxically, some of these issues might also be related to conservation successes and more bears cubs surviving.”

articles.title: What Is Behind Bangladesh’s Continuing Law and Order Crisis?
articles.full_text:
The government must rebuild public trust in the police force and insulate law enforcement from political influence.
On October 12, Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), a Bangladeshi rights organization, reported that between July and September this year, 17 people were killed and 1,227 injured in 183 incidents of political violence in Bangladesh. This was a 12 percent increase in the number of incidents in the same period last year. Mob violence also rose sharply from 98 to 137.
These figures indicate that the Bangladeshi state is struggling to stabilize and normalize the law and order situation in the country since the revolutionary mobilization in 2024. So, the transition from the previous authoritarian ecosystem under Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League to the new democratic ecosystem has faced several challenges.
According to data from the human rights organization, Ain o Salish Kendra, deaths from mob violence increased from 51 in 2023 to 128 in 2024 and 197 in 2025. Police say that registered murder cases increased from 3,023 in 2023 to 3,786 in 2025. Besides that, reports of incidents of extortion, political clashes, and armed violence have raised concerns about the deteriorating law and order situation in Bangladesh.
After the fall of Hasina’s authoritarian regime in August 2024, public ire was directed against law and enforcement authorities; 450 of Bangladesh’s 639 police stations became nonfunctional following attacks, while approximately 30 percent of police positions were left temporarily vacant.
Building trust in the police forces was a daunting task. There was little trust in the police force to begin with, thanks to the colonial policing culture that East Pakistan and then Bangladesh inherited, and even embraced. Successive regimes initially used the police as a tool not so much to enforce law and order as to stifle dissent. Political connections and corruption determined professional advancement within the police force. As a result, the Bangladesh police were hardly a professional force.
Ahead of the 2024 national election, nearly 10,000 opposition activists were arrested, while politically motivated cases, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings became recurring instruments of repression. Police authorities were reportedly involved in almost 708 enforced disappearance cases. Some also threatened women with rape if they didn’t fall in line.
The Hasina regime used the police to weaken its opponents, and as many officers became tools of the regime, the ladder to climb the ranks was less about hard work than about loyalty to the government and serving its agenda. For example, 349 police officers received awards, including one who received recognition for arresting photographer Shahidul Alam over his criticism of the government.
This broken and untrustworthy ecosystem could not be fixed in a few days, weeks or even months. When the anti-Hasina protests ended, people guarded the streets as the whole police and law-and-order maintenance system broke apart.
Even routine policing has become a challenge in Bangladesh. Officers who previously operated with strong political backing now face considerable risks when intervening in confrontations. Although the interim regime intervened to restore the law and order mechanism and revive the working of police stations, it has been difficult for people to trust the police.
The color of police uniforms and the logo of the police force were changed twice, but these superficial adjustments had little impact on how the public perceived the police.
Then came initiatives to rebuild the police force. However, a member of the Police Reform Commission that was set up post-2024 told The Diplomat that the recommendations for reforming the police have not been taken seriously by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government. It has not taken a single step towards reforming the police force, he said. As a result, public perception of the police force has not improved much. According to a survey by the International Republican Institute, 52 percent of respondents disapproved of the police’s performance, while 45 percent approved. Of all of Bangladesh’s public institutions surveyed, the police force secured the lowest public approval
Another reason for the poor law and order situation in Bangladesh is the changing structure of political authority at the grassroots level. During the Awami League’s 15 years in power, local political and economic influence was largely concentrated within very systematized networks connected to the ruling party. Control over transport terminals, markets, construction contracts, land, and other economic resources was often exercised through internally negotiated and mutually established political patronage networks. So the division and the hierarchy were clear.
The fall of the Awami League disrupted this hierarchy. Individuals and groups previously excluded from local power structures began competing for positions and resources formerly controlled by these networks. The clash for the new owner of the throne was on the table, and local political competition became intertwined with disputes over extortion, property, markets, and territorial influence. In May alone, Dhaka Metropolitan Police identified 1,280 active extortionists in the capital, including 148 armed criminals. Throughout the country, 600 incidents of political violence were documented between August 2024 and December 2025, resulting in 158 deaths and more than 7,000 injuries, where many confrontations involved struggles over local dominance and economic resources.
These rivalries have continued after the BNP formed the government in February this year. Of the 183 political-violence incidents documented by HRSS between July and September this year, 69 involved internal BNP conflicts, while another 92 involved confrontations between BNP members and other political groups.  Rival factions seeking influence within the same political organization have become an important source of conflict and violence at the grassroots level.
So, post-2024, Bangladesh has entered an endless loop of conflicts as rival political groups compete for local authority. The government seems unable to control the police, even as the latter are weak and lack the moral authority to solve the problem. And most significantly, in this process, conflicts are reinforcing each other.
It is time that the BNP government wakes up to the grave law and order situation in the country. Its immediate task should be to rebuild police authority without restoring political control over policing.
The Police Commission Ordinance adopted in December 2025, which was intended to strengthen oversight and accountability, has since ceased to have effect. This means that the legal framework designed to regulate police conduct is no longer operative, leaving oversight mechanisms unenforced. Without institutional independence, the police risk becoming dependent on political patronage again, while competition over local resources continues to encourage violence.
Establishing law and order in Bangladesh will need more than increasing police deployment or arresting individual criminals. It will require rebuilding public trust, insulating law enforcement from political influence, and preventing local groups from converting political connections into coercive economic power. Otherwise, the country risks replacing one system of politically controlled order with another, without establishing the rule of law that the July uprising promised.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Counterterrorism Campaign Is at an Inflection Point
articles.full_text:
If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the causes.
Pakistan security forces search a car in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for weapons, Oct. 18, 2026.
For the last several years, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) has been the epicenter of terrorism in Pakistan. However, 2026 marks an exception to this rule, as Balochistan has emerged as the most volatile region in terms of both the number of attacks and casualties. As of October 19, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal’s open-source data, Balochistan had suffered 1,147 terrorist attacks, and 2,394 deaths (424 civilians, 736 security personnel, and 1,233 insurgents or terrorists, plus one death that was not categorized). However, numbers provide only one aspect of a disturbing and complex security situation.
With 12 of KP’s 36 districts witnessing a worsening law-and-order situation and a receding writ of the state, Pakistan recently imposed emergency and governor’s rule in the province. Two militant networks, Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), have been carrying out large-scale attacks from their hideouts in Afghanistan and reconstituted networks in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border areas. Since the Taliban’s return to power, the organizational coherence, operational capacity, recruitment strategies, propaganda methods, and fundraising techniques of these terrorist networks have significantly evolved.
Against this backdrop, Pakistan’s counterterrorism approach must be grounded in an accurate assessment of a complex and fluid threat landscape. Taking an over-simplistic view of a complicated threat picture would result in temporary respite instead of permanent peace. Therefore, taking a holistic and nuanced view of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s security situation is the first step in restoring peace in the province.
Terrorism in KP predates the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s (PTI) three successive governments in the province. In fact, its contemporary roots can be traced to the May 1994 Malakand uprising of Sufi Muhammad’s Tehreek-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Muhammadi (TNSM). Since then, terrorism has persisted in KP in one form or another. Therefore, terrorism in the province is despite, and not because of, the PTI’s provincial regime. The PTI’s lack of cooperation is just one of the several factors that have contributed to a worsening law-and-order situation in the restive province. Nevertheless, it is quite unfortunate that the PTI politicized internal security.
Pakistan’s flawed pro-Taliban Afghan policy, kinetic-heavy counterterrorism approach, governance deficit, underdeveloped non-kinetic counterterrorism framework (or a Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism policy), and absence of structural reforms have cumulatively contributed to the current security situation in KP. If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the root causes.
Since the military is Pakistan’s most developed and capable security institution, the country has heavily leaned on it to suppress terrorism. By and large, military operations have proved successful in dismantling terrorist networks, their command-and-control nodes, organizational infrastructure, and logistical pipelines. However, the absence of political processes required to translate those tactical advantages into permanent strategic gains reversed improvements in security.
Going forward, transparent and timely strategic communication is crucial in fighting and discrediting terrorist networks. Pakistani security institutions must ensure transparent and timely communication grounded in the rule-of-law approach to reclaim the narrative domain from violent nonstate actors. They must provide a realistic assessment to the public that the military has no magic wand to bring an overnight improvement in the security situation. It will be a long struggle before peace can be restored. The first step would be to reduce the intensity of terrorist attacks and their impact. Then, large-scale kinetic operations will be required to blunt the sharp edge of terrorism.
Here, strategic communication is important. It will involve a two-pronged effort. First, the government must comprehensively address public concerns about why previous operations, despite their mixed results, were necessary. Faulting them alone for terrorism’s recurrence is unfair. The blame equally goes to the absence of political processes and good governance. There is a need for constitutional and administrative reforms too.
Second, the government must unambiguously convey to the masses how and why the new counterterrorism operations will be different from their previous iterations. Persistent and timely communication to the public will bridge the existing perception gaps about previous counterterrorism policies and their outcomes. Especially in the age of social media, terrorists are exploiting communication gaps and information blackouts. Malevolent actors jump into these situations to misguide public perception through misinformation and disinformation campaigns. Therefore, ensuring continuous and consistent communication about the progress of counter-terrorism operations and challenges confronting them will be critical.
Likewise, unlike in the past, the security institutions will do well to avoid premature victory declarations.  Such pronouncements, especially without consolidating security gains through kinetic operations into permanent strategic advantages, can result in complacency and a false sense of security. This time around, the absence of violence must not be mistaken for peace. This happened during the 2015-2020 period when a decline in terrorist attacks and the displacement of terrorist networks was confused with their elimination. The premature victory trap is tempting but dangerous, as it erodes public trust, which is central to the success of counterterrorism initiatives.
Similarly, a clear distinction between eliminating terrorists and terrorism is important. Terrorists, despite their elimination, keep returning to the battlefield as long as the roots of terrorism are not adequately tackled. Terrorism keeps the recruitment pipeline alive by exploiting ideological, political, and socioeconomic grievances. Terrorism is effectively tackled when terrorists are ideologically and discursively discredited to a point where the masses reject their appeal despite having reservations about the state. For that, strengthening state-society relations, or renewing the social contract, is important. The glue that keeps states and societies together is governance. Making state policies and administrative apparatus receptive to people’s needs and demands will drain the swamp where terrorists germinate.
Finally, terrorism in Pakistan has its internal and external dimensions. Internal consolidation against terrorist networks constitutes a necessary but not sufficient condition to overcome the challenge of terrorism. Pakistan will have to evolve a two-pronged policy, involving proactive diplomacy and coercion.
Diplomatically, Pakistan must highlight the Taliban’s support for the TTP, IMP, and Baloch separatist groups. At the same time, Pakistan should impose punitive costs on Kabul for allowing Afghanistan’s soil to be used for cross-border terrorism against it. Pakistani air strikes in Afghanistan should aim to destroy terrorist hideouts as well as the Taliban’s military capabilities to a point where they revisit their strategic calculus of supporting the TTP and IMP.
The declaration of emergency in KP marks an inflection point in the evolution of Pakistan’s counterterrorism policy. A prudent, holistic, transparent, and proactive approach with a long-term vision will deliver peace dividends. A reactive, kinetic-heavy approach, lacking concomitant non-kinetic interventions and a transparent communication strategy, will deliver short-term respite at the cost of long-term peace.

Therefore, ensuring continuous and consistent communication about the progress of counter-terrorism operations and challenges confronting them will be critical.
Likewise, unlike in the past, the security institutions will do well to avoid premature victory declarations.  Such pronouncements, especially without consolidating security gains through kinetic operations into permanent strategic advantages, can result in complacency and a false sense of security. This time around, the absence of violence must not be mistaken for peace. This happened during the 2015-2020 period when a decline in terrorist attacks and the displacement of terrorist networks was confused with their elimination. The premature victory trap is tempting but dangerous, as it erodes public trust, which is central to the success of counterterrorism initiatives.
Similarly, a clear distinction between eliminating terrorists and terrorism is important. Terrorists, despite their elimination, keep returning to the battlefield as long as the roots of terrorism are not adequately tackled. Terrorism keeps the recruitment pipeline alive by exploiting ideological, political, and socioeconomic grievances. Terrorism is effectively tackled when terrorists are ideologically and discursively discredited to a point where the masses reject their appeal despite having reservations about the state. For that, strengthening state-society relations, or renewing the social contract, is important. The glue that keeps states and societies together is governance. Making state policies and administrative apparatus receptive to people’s needs and demands will drain the swamp where terrorists germinate.
Finally, terrorism in Pakistan has its internal and external dimensions. Internal consolidation against terrorist networks constitutes a necessary but not sufficient condition to overcome the challenge of terrorism. Pakistan will have to evolve a two-pronged policy, involving proactive diplomacy and coercion.
Diplomatically, Pakistan must highlight the Taliban’s support for the TTP, IMP, and Baloch separatist groups. At the same time, Pakistan should impose punitive costs on Kabul for allowing Afghanistan’s soil to be used for cross-border terrorism against it. Pakistani air strikes in Afghanistan should aim to destroy terrorist hideouts as well as the Taliban’s military capabilities to a point where they revisit their strategic calculus of supporting the TTP and IMP.
The declaration of emergency in KP marks an inflection point in the evolution of Pakistan’s counterterrorism policy. A prudent, holistic, transparent, and proactive approach with a long-term vision will deliver peace dividends. A reactive, kinetic-heavy approach, lacking concomitant non-kinetic interventions and a transparent communication strategy, will deliver short-term respite at the cost of long-term peace.
articles.summary: If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the causes.

articles.title: After War of Words, China Says Relations With Philippines at ‘Critical Juncture’
articles.full_text:
Growing political polarization has the potential to undermine Manila’s ability to handle its ongoing maritime disputes with Beijing.
China on Friday expressed willingness to improve its relationship with the Philippines, but admitted that relations were at “an extremely sensitive and critical juncture” due to the actions of unnamed “outside forces.”
The two governments have been engaged in a war of words since Friday, when Jing Quan, China’s ambassador to Manila, declared that China could “easily win” a war with the Philippines. Jing was responding to a remark by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who the day prior described China as the lone “troublemaker” in Southeast Asia, due to its aggressive actions in contested parts of the South China Sea.
Speaking to the press after a Diliman Dialogues organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City, Jing said that the remark was “nonsense.”
“We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region,” he said. “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace. In this region, we enjoy peace.”
Asked on Friday about Ambassador Jing’s remark, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr ‌said that ⁠it “sounds very much like a threat” and that he would summon the ambassador to provide an explanation. Jing, who began his posting last December, was previously summoned by Marcos in July, after a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with the China Coast Guard at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands and the subsequent publication of a video by the state-run China Daily depicting Filipinos as monkeys and U.S. puppets.
Yesterday, the Chinese embassy issued a statement in which it said it considered the Philippines a “close neighbor and friend with deep historical and cultural ties.” It also said the Philippines need not choose between China and the United States and that the two sides “should maintain dialogue, manage differences, and expand cooperation in trade, investment, people-to-people exchanges, and law enforcement.”
At the same time, it said that China-Philippines relations were “at an extremely sensitive and critical juncture and require prudent, careful handling” and lambasted “anti-China politicians” who it said, “deliberately ignore China’s clear and consistent position on China-Philippines relations, instead twisting its words out of context and maliciously distorting the facts for political gain.”
It concluded by saying that differences “should be managed through dialogue” and that “outside forces” – i.e., the United States and its allies – “should not be allowed to steer bilateral relations toward confrontation.”
“China is ready to work with all sectors of Philippine society to promote dialogue, deepen trust, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation,” it added.
Such exchanges have taken place periodically between the two governments over the past few years, often linked to events in the South China Sea, where the two nations have overlapping maritime claims. Besides, Chinese and Philippine coast guards have engaged in a string of confrontations, some involving the use of physical force, which have pushed relations to their worst point in years.
Jing’s comments were preceded by a chain of public comments and responses emanating from the Philippines’ fractious domestic politics, hinting at the apparent growing polarization of foreign relations along partisan lines.
This began on October 6 with the airing of allegations that Chinese entities had sent just over $5 million in remittances to a Philippine company linked to the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, a major rival of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The claims, which came to light during Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial in the Senate, prompted Marcos to state that the involvement of Chinese money made the issue “a national security issue.”
“If it is true, it is a threat – a threat at the highest level to the republic,” Marcos said on October 12.
Duterte responded the same day by stating that the Philippines was becoming the main “troublemaker of Southeast Asia” by treating business ties with China as a national security concern. Teodoro’s comment about China being the main “troublemaker” in the region was a direct response to Duterte. At this point, Jing made his incautious entry into the “debate,” turning the domestic war of words into a potential diplomatic incident.
The incident is notable for what it says about how bitter political rivalries in the Philippines have the potential to impact Manila’s delicate balancing of relations with China and the United States. In late 2016, the administration of President Rodrigo Duterte, Sara’s father, initiated a bold turn toward China, downplaying maritime disputes in order to gain Chinese financial support for major infrastructure projects. The needle swung back under Marcos, who, after coming to office in 2022, strengthened the Philippines’ relationship with the United States and became much more forceful in his condemnations of Chinese behavior in the South China Sea.
There is now some danger that as the country moves toward the next presidential election in 2028, the two rival camps will come to see benefits in depicting each other as agents of foreign forces (the U.S. and China, respectively). The impacts of this could stretch beyond the periodic diplomatic incident. Indeed, they could begin to impact Manila’s ability to maintain a stable and predictable approach toward the challenges posed by China’s aggressive actions in the South China Sea.

articles.title: Deepavali vs Diwali Sparks New Political Row in Malaysia
articles.full_text:
Is the Malaysian Indian Congress using Hindu identity politics to regain its political relevance ahead of the next general election?
Deepavali rangoli artwork at Berjaya Times Square, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Nov. 11, 2012.
In India, religious sentiment has become such a fragile commodity that it can be hurt by almost anything: a joke, a film song, a movie title, or even a slogan printed on a T-shirt.
Far from India, a slight change in spelling and pronunciation has sparked a political maelstrom. In Malaysia, the Hindu festival of lights is celebrated as a public holiday. This time a controversy erupted because the traditional terminology, “Deepavali,” was not used in public greetings.
After Kuala Lumpur City Hall erected festive arches wishing the public a “Happy Diwali,” M. Saravanan, deputy president of the Malaysian Indian Congress (MIC), accused the authorities of erasing the traditional terminology. For him, the change in spelling has become a question of cultural identity and religious sentiment.
Saravanan subsequently wrote to Hannah Yeoh, minister in the Prime Minister’s Department responsible for Federal Territories, asking her to restore the legally gazetted name. He said that the choice of name was not merely a matter of semantics but one of respect for the linguistic and cultural heritage of Malaysian Hindus.
Saravanan’s objection is linked to the fact that he, like the majority of Malaysian Hindus, traces his ancestry to southern India, particularly Tamil Nadu. He says the term “Diwali” is typically associated with North India, while most southern states in India continue to use “Deepavali.”
The controversy highlights the apprehension that minorities face in any country, where tinkering with religious or cultural symbols can be seen as an attempt to dilute their identity, particularly given Malaysia’s history of ethnic tensions.
However, there is a political dimension to this debate. Critics see Saravanan’s objection as an attempt to bring back MIC in political discourse, as the party, after being drubbed in the 2018 general election, lost the sobriquet of sole representative of the country’s 2 million Hindus. Even the party’s supreme leader Samy Vellu could not retain his parliamentary seat, which he had held since 1974.
The historic 2018 election completely reshaped the political landscape. For the first time, Indian voters moved away from the MIC, in favor of Pakatan Harapan and its two main parties, the Democratic Action Party and People’s Justice Party.
Critics and political commentators argue that the MIC’s focus on semantic issues is a calculated effort to regain its relevance amid its declining influence in Malaysian politics. The “Deepavali versus Diwali” debate may generate headlines, they say, adding that the party needs to address deeper socioeconomic challenges, such as the forced relocation of Hindu temples and the long-standing economic disparities facing Malaysian Indians.

articles.title: Indonesian Stock Exchange Plunges After Fresh MSCI Downgrade Threat
articles.full_text:
Citing the lack of action on promised reforms, the global index provider has proposed demoting the country from “emerging market” to “standalone market” status.
The corporate headquarters of the Indonesia Stock Exchange in Jakarta, Indonesia, Jan. 23, 2025.
Indonesia’s stock market fell more than 11 percent on Friday, the steepest one-day drop since 1998, after the global index provider MSCI proposed the country’s removal ‌from its global stock indexes.
In a statement on Friday, MSCI said that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.”
The proposal is more serious than MSCI’s earlier threat, announced in January, to downgrade Indonesia from “emerging market” to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market. Chief among these were the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
On Friday, MSCI again cited “significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market, including persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behavior.”
MSCI said it would procure feedback from market participants until the end of April 2027, and then announce its decision by June 30.
MSCI’s role as the primary benchmark for institutional investors gives it considerable power over emerging economies. As Reuters explains, a downgrade to “standalone” status “would exclude Indonesian stocks from indexes tracked by global funds, potentially triggering billions of dollars in capital outflows.”
Markets responded to the news as one would expect, with the Jakarta Composite Index falling by 11.6 percent, losing $65 billion of value. It was the largest single-day drop since the Asian financial crisis.
After MSCI’s January announcement, which also caused a hemorrhage in Indonesian equity markets, Indonesia announced a long list of reforms to address MSCI’s concerns, including a doubling of the ​minimum free float for listed companies to 15 percent. Top executives of the exchange and regulatory body also ​stepped down.
However, in its statement on Friday, MSCI said that “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market.”
“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.”
MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”
If downgraded, Indonesia would join Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe in the standalone category, becoming both the largest economy and the only Asia-Pacific market in the grouping. MSCI has said that reclassification to “standalone” status is typically done in cases of “severe deterioration in market accessibility or size and liquidity.”
The announcement, which came ahead of MSCI’s expected verdict on Indonesia’s reclassification to “frontier” status next month, came as a shock to many observers. Rully Arya Wisnubroto, head of research at Mirae Asset Sekuritas in Jakarta, told Reuters that the proposal “goes well beyond what we had considered our worst-case scenario.” Another analyst described it as “a wake-up call for Indonesia.”
Reza Priyambada, an analyst and director at Reliance Sekuritas, told the Jakarta Globe that given the reputational impact a downgrade to “standalone” status would have, the government had to act urgently to show it was serious about reform.
“Reforms should not focus solely on market development and the enforcement of sanctions,” he told the paper. “Authorities also need to ensure a level playing field in market mechanisms and address other issues that shape international investors’ assessments of the quality of Indonesia’s capital market.”
If the government fails to stave off a downgrade, it would severely impact Indonesia’s attractiveness as a destination for foreign investment and put significant pressure on President Prabowo Subianto, whose administration has marked a break with the conservative financial stewardship of its predecessors.
Coming to office in late 2024, the former general set an ambitious goal of 8 percent annual GDP growth for the rest of his term, and has introduced a number of high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, that, along with the global spike in fuel prices, have widened the fiscal deficit. Prabowo has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s returns from natural resources and international trade.
The president’s pugnacious and highly personalized style of governance, which has affected everything from fiscal policy to foreign relations, is at the root of much investor concern. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for the country, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”
Perceptions have also been shaped by the growing sense of volatility and unpredictability in how Indonesian institutions as a whole operate. A good example is the jailing in June of Gojek co-founder Nadiem Makarim, previously a leading member of Indonesia’s tech scene, on flimsy corruption charges related to the procurement of Google Chromebooks during his time as education minister.
As one observer noted at the time, the Nadiem case confirmed many investors’ perception of Indonesia as a country where “the line between a business decision, a policy misjudgment, and a prosecutable offense is drawn after the fact by whoever holds power at the time.”
As a reflection of the general economic malaise, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June.
In addition to the aforementioned reforms, the Prabowo administration has reshuffled its economic team in a bid to restore investor confidence. In July, the governor of the central bank stepped down, followed by Prabowo’s replacement of his finance minister in September. It will no doubt also announce a host of new reforms in the days and weeks to come.
Whether all of this has much effect on MSCI’s verdict remains to be seen. Judging by the wording of its latest announcement, some kind of downgrade for Indonesia is certain; it is now merely a question of how severe the shock will be.
