articles.title: Exercise Tarang Shakti: A Mirror to India’s Multipronged Engagements
articles.full_text:
The exercise reflects two trends: the Indian military’s deepening interoperability with key partner nations, and India’s multi-vector foreign policy.
An Indian Air Force HAL Tejas leads a formation of a Mikoyan MiG-29UPG, Dassault Mirage 2000, Dassault Rafale, SEPECAT Jaguar, and Sukhoi Su-30MKI during Tarang Shakti 26 over Jodhpur, India, Oct. 2, 2026.
“The defense relationships of the future will be about technology and trust, not just about platforms,” India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said at an event and demonstration in Jodhpur on October 10 as the multilateral Exercise Tarang Shakti neared its end. A fly-past after that featured an arrow-shaped formation that included the Indian Air Force Su-30MKI (Russian origin) at the center, flanked on one side by a U.S. F-35 and an Indian Light Combat Aircraft (LCA), and on the other side by a French Rafale and an F-16 of the United Arab Emirates Air Force. This was an impressive formation; the technology and firepower they represented cannot be easily beaten.
An American fifth-generation fighter flying alongside a Russian-origin jet bears testimony to India’s multi-pronged foreign policy and military engagements.
Beyond Tarang Shakti, some bilateral exercises have culminated while others are lined up, showcasing the busy calendar of India’s military diplomacy and military-to-military engagements. For instance, at Vladivostok in Russia, the Indian and Russian Navies are holding their annual Indra exercise from October 13 to 18.
Together, these reflect two trends: one is the Indian military’s deepening interoperability across land, sea and air with key partner nations and like-minded countries, and the other is India’s multi-vectored foreign policy in line with its much-espoused strategic autonomy.
A biennial exercise, Tarang Shakti is now in its second edition.  It was themed “Power in Partnership” and was held at Jodhpur near India’s western borders. It commenced on September 26 and ended on October 12.  It brought together the Indian Air Force (IAF) and seven other countries – Australia, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, the UAE, and the U.S. – who deployed their aerial assets. Thirty-two other nations participated as observers.
The real metric of an exercise’s utility is not what the host nation deploys but what partner nations bring in, reflective of the value they see from it. The U.S. fifth-generation F-35 jets exercised over Indian skies for the first time, operating alongside the entire gamut of IAF fighters – the LCA, Rafale, SU-30MKI, Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars, French Rafales and the UAE’s F-16s. These were completed by A-400M and C-130/ C-130J transport aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, G-6000 and other support platforms. An IAF official, citing a post-exercise data brief, told The Diplomat that Tarang Shakti saw more than 800 sorties and 600 hours flown.
The U.S. Pacific Air Forces deployed six F-35A Lightning IIs and one KC-135R Stratotanker along with over 200 personnel. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, U.S. Ambassador in India Sergio Gor remarked that their F-35s do not go all over the world and termed their presence at Tarang Shakti as “another example of trust” between the two countries. France, a resident Indian Ocean power, fielded four Rafales, three A330 Phoenix aerial refuellers, two A400M transport aircraft and 300 personnel. This was part of its larger Pegase26 mission that set out on September 8, traveling across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific, Middle East and North Africa. Over 40 days across nine destinations and covering over 40,000 miles, the mission demonstrates its capacity for long-range deployment, sustenance and adaptability.
Exercises typically involve subject matter exchanges, and India, as the host nation, utilized this to brief visitors on the outcomes of Operation Sindoor of May 2025, which has generated significant operational lessons for military planners. Encapsulating this, Exercise Director Air Vice Marshal Raj Thakur noted that Operation Sindoor was one of the remarkable operations carried out by India, and there was a lot of interest in knowing about it. “And that’s why in one of the subject matter expert exchanges, we briefed them about what exactly has happened in Operation Sindoor and our part of the story, and that was very well received,” Thakur said.
India has had a very busy diplo-military calendar in recent years. These were quite often simultaneous engagements with nations that are warring or adversaries. To appreciate the busy calendar and the diversity of engagements by the Indian military, it is worth looking at some of the notable engagements since July.
The India-U.S. bilateral Army exercise Yudh Abhyas was conducted from September 15 to 27. It saw 600 personnel from each side exercise at a high-altitude area at Auli in Uttarakhand, followed by long-range firepower drills, including U.S. HIMARS, Indian Pinaka rocket systems, and counter-drone systems in action, at Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. Yudh Abhyas began in 2004 as a platoon-level exercise focused on peacekeeping operations and has since significantly expanded in scope and complexity. This is the case with all other India-U.S. military exercises: Cope India, the bilateral air exercise, or Exercise Malabar, which began as a bilateral naval exercise, have now become quadrilateral exercises featuring submarines and aircraft carriers practicing highly complex scenarios.
In addition to Yudh Abhyas, the Indian Army held bilateral wargames with Thailand (Maitree-XV), Mongolia (Nomadic Elephant), Kazakhstan (KAZIND) and UAE (Mountain Guardian), whether incoming or outgoing, with the last one set to conclude on October 18.
The Indian Navy has been the busiest with at least eight engagements. In addition to Indra, a trilateral exercise between India, Brazil and South Africa (Exercise IBSAMAR) is currently underway off South Africa. The Quad grouping, which includes India, Australia, Japan and the U.S., conducted a Tabletop Exercise on September 3 and 4 hosted by Japan to advance the Quad Indo-Pacific Logistics Network. In end-September, Quad Coast Guards carried out the second joint sail under the QUAD‑at‑Sea Ship Observer Mission. Indian Coast Guard Ship Shaunak sailed from Chennai on September 25 for Perth in Australia with six sea riders—two officers each from India and Japan, and one officer each from Australia and the U.S. embarked.
On October 8, the Indian Coast Guard conducted the 12th national Maritime Search and Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) off the coast of Odisha, which in addition to all Indian stakeholders, had 32 observers from 30 countries. It underscores the extent of deepening engagement, especially in the maritime domain, which has implications far and wide.
The IAF held two bilateral exercises with Japan (Veer Guardian) and Malaysia (Udara Shakti). More importantly, it joined the multilateral exercise Pitch Black hosted by the Royal Australian Air Force from July 7 to August 7.
The oft-repeated “interoperability” is more than just flying together in a fly past. It is extremely complex, necessitating understanding tactics, techniques, procedures, and cultural practices to seamlessly integrate the diverse range of equipment while also preserving one’s sensitive operational aspects. For instance, while the U.S. F-35s took part in war games, they were kept away from any prying eyes, even of the participating nations, highlighting the sensitivity of its most advanced technology. This prompted Air  Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh to take a friendly jibe at Gen. Kevin Schneider, the U.S. Pacific Air Forces Commander. At a press conference on October 10, the IAF chief pointed out: “Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you talk about selling it to us.”
While deepening engagements point to the evolving balancing and hedging in the Indo-Pacific, exercises are a way to prepare for evolving threats rather than be directed at anyone. This was underscored by Air Chief Singh at a press conference along with other chiefs and heads of participating forces. As far as the Indo-Pacific is concerned, the exercise was not meant to be projecting anything in any region, Singh stressed.
What do these exercises translate to in real time? As Gen. Schneider succinctly put it, “We don’t know what the security situation holds or what the future holds. Some of us may be called to do humanitarian assistance disaster relief, or there may be other challenges that we face. But when we come together, we don’t do it cold; we do it on a foundation of teamwork that is established at Tarang Shakti, Pitch Black, Red Flag Alaska, or the myriad of other exercises that take place throughout the Indo-Pacific region.”
Both Exercise Tarang Shakti and Exercise Yudh Abhyas were barometers of the extent of interoperability that has been achieved over the years by India with its key strategic partners.
The aim of Tarang Shakti was to enhance mutual understanding of tactical air power application, strengthen interoperability among participating Air Forces, and foster seamless multinational cooperation through integrated air operations, joint administration, logistics support, and maintenance coordination, a handout given at the event said. From the feedback and observations of participants, the exercise seems to have achieved what it set out to do.
It only reiterates India’s continuing expansion of military-to-military engagements in various formats and across geographies in line with its strategic objectives and in turn, the outcomes shaping the objectives.
“The defense relationships of the future will be about technology and trust, not just about platforms,” India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said at an event and demonstration in Jodhpur on October 10 as the multilateral Exercise Tarang Shakti neared its end. A fly-past after that featured an arrow-shaped formation that included the Indian Air Force Su-30MKI (Russian origin) at the center, flanked on one side by a U.S. F-35 and an Indian Light Combat Aircraft (LCA), and on the other side by a French Rafale and an F-16 of the United Arab Emirates Air Force. This was an impressive formation; the technology and firepower they represented cannot be easily beaten.
An American fifth-generation fighter flying alongside a Russian-origin jet bears testimony to India’s multi-pronged foreign policy and military engagements.
Beyond Tarang Shakti, some bilateral exercises have culminated while others are lined up, showcasing the busy calendar of India’s military diplomacy and military-to-military engagements. For instance, at Vladivostok in Russia, the Indian and Russian Navies are holding their annual Indra exercise from October 13 to 18.
Together, these reflect two trends: one is the Indian military’s deepening interoperability across land, sea and air with key partner nations and like-minded countries, and the other is India’s multi-vectored foreign policy in line with its much-espoused strategic autonomy.
A biennial exercise, Tarang Shakti is now in its second edition.  It was themed “Power in Partnership” and was held at Jodhpur near India’s western borders. It commenced on September 26 and ended on October 12.  It brought together the Indian Air Force (IAF) and seven other countries – Australia, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, the UAE, and the U.S. – who deployed their aerial assets. Thirty-two other nations participated as observers.
The real metric of an exercise’s utility is not what the host nation deploys but what partner nations bring in, reflective of the value they see from it. The U.S. fifth-generation F-35 jets exercised over Indian skies for the first time, operating alongside the entire gamut of IAF fighters – the LCA, Rafale, SU-30MKI, Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars, French Rafales and the UAE’s F-16s. These were completed by A-400M and C-130/ C-130J transport aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, G-6000 and other support platforms. An IAF official, citing a post-exercise data brief, told The Diplomat that Tarang Shakti saw more than 800 sorties and 600 hours flown.
The U.S. Pacific Air Forces deployed six F-35A Lightning IIs and one KC-135R Stratotanker along with over 200 personnel. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, U.S. Ambassador in India Sergio Gor remarked that their F-35s do not go all over the world and termed their presence at Tarang Shakti as “another example of trust” between the two countries. France, a resident Indian Ocean power, fielded four Rafales, three A330 Phoenix aerial refuellers, two A400M transport aircraft and 300 personnel. This was part of its larger Pegase26 mission that set out on September 8, traveling across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific, Middle East and North Africa. Over 40 days across nine destinations and covering over 40,000 miles, the mission demonstrates its capacity for long-range deployment, sustenance and adaptability.
Exercises typically involve subject matter exchanges, and India, as the host nation, utilized this to brief visitors on the outcomes of Operation Sindoor of May 2025, which has generated significant operational lessons for military planners. Encapsulating this, Exercise Director Air Vice Marshal Raj Thakur noted that Operation Sindoor was one of the remarkable operations carried out by India, and there was a lot of interest in knowing about it. “And that’s why in one of the subject matter expert exchanges, we briefed them about what exactly has happened in Operation Sindoor and our part of the story, and that was very well received,” Thakur said.
articles.summary: The exercise reflects two trends: the Indian military’s deepening interoperability with key partner nations, and India’s multi-vector foreign policy.

articles.title: Cambodia’s NGO Sector Is Collapsing. Does It Matter?
articles.full_text:
Imported by international donors in the 1990s, NGOs have supplanted rather than strengthened local forms of political organizing.
A dusty road in Treak village, Siem Reap province, Cambodia.
From the early 1990s through the early 2010s, Cambodia hosted one of the most vibrant, generously funded, and unchecked civil society ecosystems in Southeast Asia. Former Prime Minister Hun Sen once famously referred to the country as a “heaven for NGOs.” And indeed, up to 6,100 registered non-government organizations (NGOs) and associations have been able to flourish, including about 3,450 NGOs and 2,650 other civil society associations. This number of NGOs is very high by global standards, by one count making up the second highest number per capita in the world after Rwanda.
A confluence of disasters has changed all that. The heyday for NGOs effectively started closing following the 2013 national elections, when the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) faced a major electoral threat and began systematically dismantling the public sphere. Viewing NGOs as a vehicle for hostile foreign-backed “color revolutions,” the Cambodian government introduced a restrictive and controversial Law on Associations and Non-Governmental Organizations in 2015. It also began to use tax audits, lawsuits, and political pressure – such as monitoring or disturbing civil society meetings, refusing to give permission for activities, and other coercive tactics – to restrict the sector.
Not only are NGOs required to navigate a suspicious and unfriendly political environment, but they also face a critically strained financial environment. Recently, the international development landscape has endured its steepest funding decline on record. As global power relations go through a process of significant reconfiguration and Cambodia simultaneously moves toward graduating from Least Developed Country status in 2029, global official development aid has been dramatically curtailed. This is set to continue.
The dramatic reduction in funds has had a significant and increasing impact on Cambodia and its NGOs. Already 10 years have passed since funding for Cambodian NGOs reached its peak in 2016. A recent survey of civil society organizations in Cambodia revealed that 26 percent of NGOs say they are not financially viable beyond 2027. It is not unreasonable to suggest that only one in five NGOs may survive the next decade.
In response to this calamity, there have been calls to redesign the ecosystem of civil society in Cambodia. These are led by the Cooperation Committee of Cambodia (CCC), which serves as the professional association of NGOs. A roadmap prepared by the CCC points to how major transformation can be achieved. Options being considered include increased reliance on local philanthropy; the reinvention of NGOs as social enterprises or technical assistance offices; blended financing; increased sharing of resources and organizational infrastructure; and, if there is interest, mergers.
If undertaken, these initiatives would together mark a profound shift away from traditional NGO models toward leaner, more specialized structures grounded in local ownership.
First, local philanthropy is captured almost exclusively by the CPP and, for the purposes of making merit, by pagodas and other institutions associated with Buddhist practice. There is little appetite among everyday citizens for giving to NGOs, and it seems unreasonable to expect NGOs to try and compete with entrenched political parties and organized religion in their fundraising efforts. A notable exception to NGOs’ failure to inspire local giving is the Cambodian Red Cross, which is skilled at generating significant donations from wealthy individuals. While this is a large and prominent humanitarian organization in Cambodia specializing in disaster relief, it is also compromised by political entanglements – its president is Hun Sen’s wife Bun Rany – and is the recipient of questionable major donations.
In any event, international philanthropy sometimes funds the wrong things, as any effective altruist will tell you. Well-meaning donors tend to give to projects that look good or feel good, not necessarily those that do good. Just this week, Sunrise Cambodia, a Cambodian NGO that has traditionally been very successful at fundraising in Australia, was in the news again after a former chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered charity raising funds for Sunrise Cambodia, was found dead after being charged with possessing child abuse materials. Financial support for Sunrise Cambodia will reportedly continue.
Second, there is no demonstrable demand for technical assistance offices or social enterprises on a scale that may mop up excess NGO programs and human resources. To date, no evidence has emerged that presents a sensible business case for this model of transforming NGOs.
Third, blended finance models may be excellent for particular types of NGOs, such as larger organizations working in agriculture, water, sanitation and hygiene, and health. But it is not a suitable approach for smaller, grassroots NGOs and those that have adopted strong social welfare, human rights, and poverty alleviation mandates. Expectations of financial return sit awkwardly alongside such priorities.
Fourth, sharing of resources is laudable, but it will not magically make more funds appear. Local NGOs tend not to take the sort of decisive and strategic action that would support mergers, and there are simply no examples of local NGOs in Cambodia merging. Some, like the author, might wish to see the CCC and the NGO Forum on Cambodia merge and show other local NGOs how it can be done. However, this would require high levels of sustained support, including access to legal advice, and advice about governance and organizational structure, human resource management and change management, and program delivery, among other things.
It is unclear if international NGOs and other donors will have an interest in supporting local NGOs with such logistics when the prospect of a merger starts to become more real. Of course, international NGOs can and do rationalize themselves at scale – consider, for example, how Oxfam and ActionAid continue to consolidate administrative functions at regional levels, how Corus International formed, and how Save the Children absorbed Merlin – but this is not a pathway that is visible nor even conceivable to local actors. For the most part, merging is akin to death. Certainly, mergers are anathema to the idea that NGOs bring income and status to their founders and leaders.
A bigger and more important question is: are NGOs really worth saving? The answer to this is not straightforward. Let’s remember that NGOs are not the center of the civil society ecosystem in Cambodia. NGOs were imported by international donors and shaped in their own image. They have a short history and are not indigenous to Cambodia. The functional equivalent of Western-style civil society in Cambodia is the intersecting business and political networks and complex patron-client ties that dominate Cambodian society. NGOs have supplanted rather than augmented or strengthened local forms of organizing. Community members are unlikely to regard NGOs as capable of representing them. NGOs are attentive to what powerful actors such as international donors, the Cambodian government and, to a lesser degree, service users and community constituents expect of them, which means they are less adept at leading societal change on their own terms.
However, there are some NGOs that can be regarded as essential. NGOs that focus on human rights and advocacy such as Licadho, Equitable Cambodia, or COMFREL should be a priority for international donors, as it seems highly unlikely that they will secure sufficient income from local philanthropy or national government grants.
It is entirely possible that large numbers of NGOs have already collapsed. Informal advice is that many of the supposed 3,450 NGOs are no longer functioning but are either unable or unwilling to deregister themselves. The collapse of NGOs will thus remain largely invisible. The Cambodian government makes it difficult to deregister NGOs; there is no clear process for doing this. Moreover, it serves the government’s purposes to be able to point to a large number of NGOs as evidence of a supportive and enabling environment for civil society. This has the potential to deflect any criticism that may arise in response to further crackdowns on civil society.
What should we expect then? And what is to be done? It is true that the future is bleak and adaptation is required. The CPP has tried and tested strategies that have proven successful in exactly these types of situations. The trade union movement and media organizations have been undercut and diminished with the entry of government-supported institutions into their respective spaces. If the playbook is followed again, it seems likely that a rise in the number of government-organized NGOs (GONGOs) will also follow in Cambodia.
In this light, a more realistic roadmap for NGOs in Cambodia may involve calculated and conditional acceptance of the demise of NGOs. It may be appropriate to learn from the experiences of the trade union movement and media outlets. It could also be necessary to cede space to GONGOs and look for opportunities to collaborate with and strengthen them. In particular, this could involve working to transfer knowledge that has been accumulated by NGOs in recent decades – including the human resources that hold such knowledge – to the emerging GONGOs.
Finally, it may be necessary to return to older models of civil society that privilege hyper-local community-based care, perhaps linked to Buddhist pagodas or other community-based institutions. In particular, this could involve systematically transferring assets and other remaining resources held by NGOs to smaller community-based organizations in rural areas. articles.title: Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN
articles.full_text:
The creation of the body, which comes ahead of next month’s ASEAN Summit in Manila, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the bloc.
Myanmar’s empty seat, as seen during the 40th ASEAN Summit (Plenary Session) in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Nov. 11, 2022.
Myanmar’s military-backed government has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee in order to support its efforts to reintegrate itself into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The Southeast Asian bloc has excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since late 2021, due to its failure to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus plan. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.
The Irrawaddy reported yesterday that the new body, which met for the first time on Tuesday, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit next month, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the 11-nation organization. Tuesday’s meeting was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and attended by representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare.
Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” from ASEAN since 2021, The Irrawaddy reported. The meeting also discussed “Myanmar‑led approaches” for restoring the country’s position in the bloc.
Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government has launched a diplomatic charm offensive, involving visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.
A priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Many of the latter’s member states appear to be supportive of Naypyidaw’s goal, and five of them – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
The Philippines also appears to be softening. In a recent interview, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN for 2026, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.
At the same time as it has wooed individual ASEAN member states, the military-backed government has forcefully rejected the Five-Point Consensus. In July, Myanmar’s military proxy parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, which “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” Min Aung Hlaing said in a speech the following month that some member states had “adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar.”
While most member states are now leaning in the direction of reopening ASEAN’s door to Myanmar – Thailand and Malaysia have both explicitly stated that this is their goal, and Singapore and Timor-Leste appear to be the last hold-outs – full normalization, like all ASEAN decisions, will require a consensus among all 11 member states. As I noted earlier this week, however, there are “evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end.”
Unless ASEAN agrees to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether, normalization would seem to require at least some effort to implement it, however nominal. With the Myanmar military ramping up its attacks on resistance groups and civilian populations accused of harboring them, this seems unlikely in the current circumstances.

articles.title: Indonesian President Replaces Head of Disaster Management Agency
articles.full_text:
The move comes amid growing scrutiny of Jakarta’s response to the forest and peatland fires that have drastically reduced air quality across the region.
Haze obscures the skyline of Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Sep. 18, 2026.
Indonesia’s President ​Prabowo Subianto yesterday replaced the head of the country’s disaster management agency in a bid to restore confidence in the government’s ability to bring intensifying land and forest fires under control.
Lt.-Gen. Kristomei Sianturi, 50, was sworn in as the chief of the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) at the State Palace in Jakarta, replacing Lt.-Gen. Suharyanto. Speaking after the ceremony, the two-star army general said that Prabowo had given him orders to move as quickly as possible to bring the fires under control.
“The directive is clear: keep pushing forward and start your duties promptly,” he said, according to Kompas. “The target is as soon as possible, because the people are already affected.”
Kristomei said that he would review the BNPB’s response procedures to ensure faster action during disasters and prevent avoidable deaths.
“Responsiveness must be measured in minutes, not hours. That is what we will evaluate going forward, so there are no more unnecessary casualties,” he said.
No official reason was given for Suharyanto’s replacement, but the change came a day after the outgoing BNPB chief’s younger brother was arrested over alleged corruption involving emergency relief funds, the Straits Times reported. The Corruption Eradication Commission said that the investigation centers on BNPB’s ready-to-use emergency funds, which are used to meet urgent needs during disasters, but did not say whether money intended to fight the forest fires was misappropriated.
Kristomei’s appointment – the second major change to Prabowo’s cabinet since the appointment of a new foreign minister on October 1 – is also likely intended to reassure Indonesia’s neighbors that it remains committed to fighting the wildfires that are currently raging on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. The forest and peatland fires have created a thick toxic haze that has darkened the skies above Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Timor-Leste, Brunei, and parts of the Philippines, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.
As the haze has persisted, Jakarta has become the focus of increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires, many of which Indonesian officials admit were lit deliberately to clear agricultural land. As I noted yesterday, Social media users in Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia have become increasingly angry at Jakarta’s response to the fires, with some Indonesian netizens even urging Singapore and Malaysia to impose sanctions on their own government.
Meanwhile, politicians in Malaysia have called for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government to lodge formal diplomatic complaints with Jakarta, and the country’s foreign minister said that he plans to raise the issue at an upcoming meeting of his ASEAN counterparts.
Yesterday, after air quality readings in some parts of Singapore reached the worst levels in more than a decade, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires in Indonesia.
“Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and explore joint action with other countries,” he said on social media.
Under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, passed in 2014, Singaporean authorities can take legal action against companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in Singapore, even if their activities take place overseas. History suggests that Singapore will refrain from confronting Indonesia directly over the haze issue, but the fact that Wong raised the prospect of investigations is a sign of the government’s growing frustration with its large neighbor.
Indonesia has announced a number of other measures designed to combat the fires. Prabowo yesterday approved foreign assistance for its fire-fighting efforts, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said yesterday. “The president has also given his approval, and discussions are now underway at the technical level. In this case, the technical discussions are being handled by BNPB,” he said at a closed-door meeting.
“What we need to emphasize is that this is a matter of great seriousness and is receiving the President’s direct attention,” Arrmanatha said, although he did not specify which countries had offered assistance or what form the assistance would take.
Also yesterday, the BBC reported that aircraft were deployed to scatter pellets of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions most affected by the haze. Indonesian police have also named more than 200 people and nine companies as suspects in forest and land fire investigations across the country.
Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political analyst at the National Research and Innovation Agency, told the Straits Times that the fires had “damaged the government’s image” within ASEAN, and that the reappointment of the BNPB head was “certainly part of efforts to restore the government’s image domestically and internationally.”
One way or another, the current fires will come to an end. Whether Indonesia succeeds in winning back the confidence of its neighbors will also depend on whether it puts in place policies and structures that can prevent a recurrence of a similar crisis in future.

articles.title: After 8 Months in Power, How Much Has the BNP Changed Bangladesh?
articles.full_text:
It remains to be seen how willing the new government is to change the institutions that it now controls.
Tarique Rahman takes the oath of office as Bangladesh’s prime minister at the National Parliament Complex, Dhaka, Bangladesh, Feb. 17, 2026.
Tarique Rahman had been Bangladesh’s prime minister for just 11 days when war broke out in the Middle East. He took office on February 17; on February 28, the United States and Israel attacked Iran. By March, disrupted fuel supplies had forced Bangladesh to introduce rationing, putting further pressure on its economy.
Eight months into Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) rule, the results are mixed. Remittances have risen and inflation has eased. But living costs keep rising, businesses remain cautious, and law and order remains a concern. Mob violence continues.
The government inherited serious problems, but its decisions also need to be examined. Constitutional reforms endorsed in a referendum alongside February’s national election remain under negotiation. New rights laws have drawn criticism for weakening independent oversight.
How far is the BNP willing to change the institutions it now controls? And are its decisions making people’s lives better, safer, and freer than before?
Law and order remains a concern eight months into BNP rule. According to monthly data from Bangladesh Police, the force registered fewer murder, robbery, and kidnapping cases between March and September than during the same months in 2025. Burglary cases, however, increased, while mob killings continued.
Police recorded 2,122 murder cases during these eight months, down from 2,317 a year earlier. Robbery cases fell from 1,159 to 1,077, while kidnapping cases declined slightly, from 628 to 618. Burglary cases rose from 1,796 to 2,022, an increase of nearly 13 percent.
The total number of registered cases increased by 14 percent, from 110,296 to 125,763. Narcotics cases accounted for about 90 percent of that increase, rising from 31,111 to 45,091. The increase alone cannot establish whether drug offenses became more common or police became more active in registering them.
Mob violence remained a serious concern. A comparison of cumulative reports from Ain o Salish Kendra, a human rights organization in Dhaka, gives a toll of 131 people killed in mob beatings between March and August 2026.
On April 11, a mob killed a Sufi spiritual leader in Kushtia’s Daulatpur upazila following allegations that he had insulted religion. His shrine was vandalized and set on fire. Media reports said law enforcement personnel were present but failed to control the attack.
Similar incidents occurred in Dhaka in September. On September 25, more than 200 masked attackers looted and demolished the Radda MCH-FP Center, a maternal and child healthcare facility in Dhaka. A preliminary police investigation found that officers were present but failed to stop the looting. 
A day later, hundreds of attackers stormed a property and vandalized content creator Salman Muqtadir’s studio. Police linked the attack to a land dispute involving the property owner.
Police officers themselves have also faced violence. In June, a mob assaulted two officers in Savar and freed a suspect. In July, three police officers were attacked in Kutubdia while taking a suspect into custody. On September 5, Special Branch Sub-Inspector Altaf Hossain was beaten to death in Savar. More recently, on October 10, a police inspector was seriously injured in an attack by muggers in Khulna.
The government says the police are recovering. On August 26, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed claimed that suspects in almost all criminal cases filed during the government’s first six months had been arrested within a reasonable time. He said the administration had inherited a fragile security situation and was working to improve police morale.
Extortion also remained a concern. Court records cited in media reporting show that 723 extortion cases were filed across 49 police stations in Dhaka between January and August, a period that includes several weeks before the BNP took office. 
Dr. Md Tawohidul Haque, an associate professor and crime analyst at the Institute of Social Welfare and Research, University of Dhaka, described the government’s law and order record as mixed. “We cannot say that there has been any significant improvement compared with the previous one and a half years. At the same time, we cannot say that the situation has deteriorated dramatically,” he told The Diplomat. 
Haque attributed the lack of progress partly to uneven enforcement and the government’s failure to control its own personnel: “Unless a political party takes a firm position against wrongdoing within its own ranks, the situation will not improve.”
Haque also questioned whom drug enforcement was reaching. While drug users, small retailers, and couriers faced arrest, he said, influential figures continued to benefit from political protection. “The real patrons and powerful figures behind the drug trade remain beyond the reach of the law,” he argued 
Addressing that protection would require deeper changes in policing. “The Bangladesh Police has still not been depoliticized,” Haque said. “Its internal structure also remains largely unchanged.”
Inflation eased during the BNP’s first months in office, but the improvement was uneven. In March, consumer prices were 8.71 percent higher than a year earlier. Inflation climbed to 9.42 percent in May before falling to 8.34 percent in September, barely below the 8.36 percent recorded in September 2025. Prices were still rising, adding to costs households had already absorbed.
Earnings offered little protection. In August, the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ wage index rose by 8.05 percent, trailing inflation. The index covers selected lower-paid occupations, including agricultural laborers, construction workers, and transport workers. For these workers, the figures suggest that wages still bought less than a year earlier, despite the slowdown in price increases.
There was more encouraging news from Bangladeshis working abroad. Remittances reached $18.94 billion between March and August, up 13.1 percent from the same months in 2025, according to Bangladesh Bank. These inflows helped replenish foreign exchange reserves and supported families receiving money from overseas. The improvement continued a rise in remittances that had begun before the BNP took office.
Businesses remained cautious. Bankers interviewed by The Business Standard (TBS), a Bangladeshi daily, described weak demand, expensive borrowing and energy shortages. Sohail R. K. Hussain, managing director of Bank Asia, told TBS that factories had unused capacity, giving businesses little reason to invest in expansion. The return of an elected government has yet to produce a strong recovery in borrowing.
The government inherited much of this difficulty. Bangladesh Bank had maintained tight monetary policy, while loan defaults continued to constrain lending. Its July–December policy statement acknowledged that higher interest rates alone could not resolve inflation caused by problems in markets and supply chains. It also announced a 600 billion taka financing package for industry, agriculture, and smaller businesses.
Fuel costs brought another setback in September. The government raised diesel prices from 115 to 135 taka a liter as the Middle East conflict drove up international energy costs. The Energy Ministry said the increase was needed to reduce losses at the state petroleum corporation. For businesses and households, it threatened further increases in production and transport costs, making the recent easing of inflation harder to sustain.
The government is also struggling to fund its spending plans. Banik Barta, a Bangladeshi daily, reported that the record 9.38 trillion taka budget relies on collecting nearly 7 trillion taka in revenue. Yet collections are falling as economic activity slows. 
Citing National Board of Revenue sources, the newspaper said revenue in July–August stood at 518.9 billion taka, down from 547.7 billion a year earlier and 291.6 billion below the target for those two months. Meanwhile, higher energy import costs, subsidies, increased public sector salaries, and major project commitments are adding to expenditure.
Dr. Khondaker Golam Moazzem, an industrial economist, policy analyst, and president of the Knowledge Hub Institute, said that high inflation, weak growth, and rising unemployment pointed to economic stagnation. He argued that the government had shown too little interest in the structural reforms needed for recovery. “The problem is that the government does not have the revenue support required to finance these activities,” he told The Diplomat, referring to its expanding spending commitments.
Moazzem questioned the timing of salary increases for government employees and large projects that he believed could be postponed. One such example is the large expansion of Biman Bangladesh Airlines’ fleet. Its orders for 25 Boeing aircraft from the United States and 10 Airbus jets from the European Union would total 35 new aircraft, compared with its current fleet of just 19. Moazzem warned that without reforms to the airline’s management and service quality, the massive purchases could leave Biman with a long-term debt burden that would be difficult to service.
articles.summary: It remains to be seen how willing the new government is to change the institutions that it now controls.

articles.title: Clean Energy Must Avoid the Mistake of Overdependence
articles.full_text:
The world must diversify its energy dependence, not simply relocate it from the Middle East to China.
For decades, energy security has meant oil. Countries worried about their dependence on the Middle East and Russia, the security of shipping lanes, and the geopolitical consequences of relying on a small number of producers for the oil that powered global economies. The transition to renewable energy was supposed to rebalance that equation. Yet in doing so, we may be creating a potentially greater vulnerability, since the clean energy supply chain is dominated by China.
Take Europe as an example. The year before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s natural gas imports. The war has forced European countries to scramble for new energy sources. 
The war in the Middle East showed again how quickly concentrated energy supplies can become an economic liability. Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz – or did, before the strait was effectively closed by the conflict.
Clean energy can reduce exposure to these specific chokepoints, but the world must diversify its energy dependence without simply relocating it.
China leads in the industries powering the next phase of the global economy. It is the world’s largest supplier and exporter of green technology. In July 2026, China’s green energy exports rose 51 percent year-on-year, with new energy vehicles rising an astonishing 90 percent.
China dominates the clean energy value chain. Today, the country provides roughly 85 percent of global solar production capacity and 80 percent of lithium-ion batteries. This is essentially a monopoly. In electric vehicles, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global production in 2025.
Its control also extends upstream. China holds critical positions in processing and refining the minerals essential to new energy technologies, from batteries to electric motors and wind turbines. It also possesses much of the manufacturing expertise – and increasingly the equipment – needed to turn those materials into finished products.
Therefore, clean energy dependence extends across an entire industrial ecosystem – from processing through technology, components and manufacturing equipment to the finished product. A disruption at any point in the supply chain could reverberate through the entire system. 
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that each month of a halt in Chinese battery supply chain exports could reduce output from EV factories elsewhere by some $17 billion, with more than half of those losses occurring in Europe.
The risk is not hypothetical. China’s use of export controls on rare earths and other critical materials has demonstrated how concentrated supply chains translate into strategic leverage. China mines roughly 60 percent of the world’s rare earths but produces about 90 percent of its rare earth permanent magnets, leaving downstream manufacturers with few immediate alternatives.
Oil reserves are fixed by geology, while China’s dominance in clean technology is the product of industrial policy, capital investment, and accumulated manufacturing expertise. That should, in theory, make clean energy dependence more reversible. In practice, however, diversification is difficult. 
A critical part of China’s advantage is manufacturing efficiency. The IEA attributed more than 40 percent of China’s battery cost edge over Europe to automation and efficiency. In critical mineral mining and refining, China’s position also rests on decades of accumulated processing capacity and a willingness to bear environmental costs that many other countries have been reluctant to accept. None of this can be replicated quickly.
China’s enormous investment and innovation in clean technology has helped drive down costs and accelerate deployment. Attempting to exclude China entirely would make the energy transition slower and more expensive. Interdependence is not the problem, and energy security has never required producing everything at home. It requires enough diversity that no single supplier can disrupt the system.
As with trade, the answer is not decoupling but diversification.
Countries should identify where domestic capacity is strategically necessary, build alternative sources of supply with allies and emerging markets, and continue trading and investing with China where it makes economic sense. 
It can be done, but it takes time, capital, and political will. Las Vegas-based MP Materials operates North America’s only rare earth mine of scale, producing more than 10 percent of global rare earth supply. The company is building heavy rare earth processing capacity and investing more than $1.25 billion in a magnet manufacturing campus. Importantly, its strategy is becoming international: in 2025, MP Materials, the U.S. government, and Saudi Arabia’s Maaden agreed to develop a Saudi rare earth refinery to supply rare earth oxides to U.S., Saudi, and allied manufacturers.
This one refinery is not, on its own, a solution, but it points to the kind of allied, government-supported investment in processing that rebalancing requires.
While the world will remain dependent upon fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, the diversification to clean energy will continue, and the stakes will rise as demand grows. The world should not spend decades reducing its dependence on Middle Eastern and Russian hydrocarbons only to discover that it has exchanged one form of strategic dependence for another – this time on China.

articles.title: Nepal Should Not Shoulder the Himalayan Climate Crisis Alone
articles.full_text:
“No matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.”
Have you wondered why the current global order expects frontline geographies to absorb the astronomical shocks of climate disasters entirely on their own, especially when those very states face the unprecedented brunt of a crisis born from a total failure of global collective action? Who funds the recovery when the baseline geography of a nation is structurally altered overnight, especially when the crisis is entirely outside of their own making?
Of course, Nepal’s civilizational history has been a long, adaptive iteration to deal with an unforgiving topography and the sheer gravity of terrains that constantly pull everything down. But the scale of what we saw on August 26, 2026 was entirely unprecedented. The staggering images of landscapes dissolving that looked like a terrifying sci-fi reel made rounds among global audiences, 
Seven weeks have passed since a massive rockslide detached from a high mountain face in northern Nepal’s Langtang Lirung massif, slamming into the glacial lake below and triggering a catastrophic debris torrent along the Rasuwa-Trishuli corridor. The mud remains heavy, unyielding, and thick with the wreckage of a singular, devastating event. Ever since that unimaginable disaster, Nepal has grappled with the heartbreaking loss of close to 1,500 lives. Thousands remain missing. And thousands more are desperately trying to rebuild their shattered lives from scratch.
The loss is vast. And that stretches far beyond human lives and the statistical tallies of washed-away bridges and infrastructural damages. Or of erased roads or buried houses.
Take the sudden megawatt loss of hydropower assets clustered along this single corridor, projects that were either already online delivering power or actively under construction. Cumulatively, this single cascading hazard knocked over 400 megawatts of clean energy offline in a single afternoon. This is a fundamental blow to a country that has courageously looked toward a future of 30,000 megawatts of clean energy capacity by the next decade. Crucially, much of that power was not meant for domestic consumption alone but was strategically destined to flow southward across the border to anchor the green transitions of our neighbors too. The disaster wiped out roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s total installed electrical capacity in a single afternoon; that does more than disrupt domestic energy equations. 
The damage also includes the immediate destruction of the primary cross-border trade artery to our northern neighbor, China, the vital and the nearest entry point for the electric vehicles driving Nepal’s national green transition. Against all conventional global assumptions, Nepal has emerged as a global leader in green mobility, with new passenger EV adoption skyrocketing past 75 percent as the nation aggressively pursues the goal of becoming a fully electric economy. These efforts have now been paralyzed.
Even more devastating is what this corridor represents to the human spirit, and to our resilient high mountain communities. The tragedy impacted the sacred artery for international pilgrims journeying toward the ancient Kailash-Mansarovar sanctuary, a landscape deeply revered across Hindu and Buddhist civilizations, and a legendary frontier of adventure for global explorers. Tragically, many of those currently dead or missing under the mud include these very pilgrims and tourists. 
By flattening connecting bridges, stranding cross-border travelers, and decimating localized ecotourism infrastructure, these disasters have dismantled the historic human and economic ties and spiritual sanctuary of the region that bind South Asian nations together, directly threatening the collective dream of an interconnected green grid.
Then came September. Then came October. And both months bought multi-front disasters that defied everything we thought we could predict.
In September, extreme late-monsoon saturation triggered massive landslides across multiple districts simultaneously, repeatedly snapping grid transmission lines and fracturing vital economic corridors just as fast as recovery teams could repair them. 
October stripped away any remaining illusion of predictability. On October 11, a morning landslide and the subsequent breach of the natural dam along the steep Budhigandaki River corridor in central Nepal, west of Kathmandu, did more than wash away roads. The landslide slammed directly into the construction site of the 341 MW plant down the valley, specifically engineered to run off the river’s natural flow and step in during our hours of highest electricity demand. While the major structure was not entirely wiped away, the impact leaves us with fundamental questions about systemic safety, early warning capabilities, and the steep costs of re-engineering our infrastructure for a volatile future. 
Ultimately, if these vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the cascading risks will not stop at our borders; they will inevitably strip the entire region of the very clean energy opportunities needed to power our collective green transition.
Nepal, of course, has a lot of serious reflection to do regarding its own development thinking; we are by no means oblivious to that. But the broader crisis remains clear, because no matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.
This gives immediate, painful validation to the warning delivered by Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Addressing the international community, the prime minister laid bare a grim economic reality, warning that physical recovery from these escalating disasters could consume up to 10 percent of Nepal’s national GDP. For a nation that contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, isn’t this far more than a localized setback? Is it not a crushing, completely unjust financial penalty imposed by an unequal global architecture?
Why should a frontline nation independently underwrite the immense physical and financial risks of cross-border infrastructure that the entire subcontinent’s survival depends on? Rather than pointing fingers among ourselves, isn’t this a definitive wake-up call for all of us in the region to come together, align our strategies, and act as a unified front? If our collective green future is at stake, is this massive burden truly for Nepal to shoulder alone, or is it the ultimate test of shared regional solidarity and global accountability?
As we prepare to gather next month at the U.N. Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Nepal will undoubtedly be discussed as a definitive case study. But what will the optics of that discussion be? Will we once again be treated as a passive, flat statistic on a ledger, or as a living warning of what happens when climate shocks freeze a real-world green transition?
The current global climate financing architecture remains stubbornly blind to the high-velocity crises of the Himalayas. If a nation that did everything right, pioneering citizen-funded hydro-infrastructure and skyrocketing its EV adoption, can have its clean energy core paralyzed in a single afternoon, who is it that truly needs to change? Is it Nepal that must reshape its ambitions, or is it a broken global financial system that must finally overhaul its slow-moving bureaucracy before the millions who revere and depend on these ecosystems downstream pay the ultimate price?

articles.title: China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea
articles.full_text:
The rise of seabed mining will add new complexity to the South China Sea disputes.
In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.
The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.
For now, China’s rare earth strategy and its South China Sea strategy remain largely distinct. China’s leverage in rare earths comes less from pure geology than from the country’s dominant position in refining, separation, and magnet production, combined with regulatory instruments that allow Beijing to manage outward flows of selected minerals. The April 2025 export control measures on several medium and heavy rare-earth-related items underscored how critical minerals have become part of China’s national security toolbox. 
By contrast, the South China Sea has traditionally been discussed and understood through a different strategic vocabulary: sovereignty claims, maritime jurisdiction, military presence, fisheries, hydrocarbons, and sea lanes of communication. This kind of separation, however, may not hold indefinitely, because the critical minerals competition is acquiring an increasingly prominent maritime dimension. 
As governments search for ways to reduce dependence on existing rare earth supply chains, attention is gradually shifting toward deep-sea muds, polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts, and other seabed resources. These resources are not immediate substitutes for today’s land-based mines and processing systems, but they are entering strategic planning and industrial policy. Once critical minerals are imagined not only as terrestrial commodities but also as seabed resources, the boundary between resource security and maritime security begins to blur.
The South China Sea disputes have always had a strategic dimension, in addition to the sovereignty disputes alone. Yet oil, gas, fisheries, and shipping are the dominant drivers of maritime competition; seabed resources have thus far remained a less developed part of the story. Studies of Fe-Mn crusts and polymetallic nodules in the South China Sea have identified the presence of cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, yttrium, and other critical materials. 
That does not mean that the South China Sea is about to become a commercially viable rare earth mining zone. But as deep-sea mineral technologies and governance frameworks mature, the South China Sea’s significance may be reinterpreted through the language of critical minerals security.
That shift, if it occurs, would not replace the existing logic of South China Sea competition but add another layer to it. Critical minerals could make seabed mapping, marine scientific research, environmental regulation, and deep-sea mining rules more politically sensitive. Activities that once appeared primarily scientific or commercial could come to be viewed through the lens of supply chain resilience and national security. 
China is especially well placed to think across these domains because it already possesses capabilities on both sides of the equation. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench.

China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench. 
Rare earths are not about to become the central driver of South China Sea disputes. The more important trend is that two strategic arenas for competition are beginning to converge. China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. As critical minerals competition expands offshore, these two forms of strategic control may begin to interact. The South China Sea, in the longer term, may become part of a broader debate over who maps, governs, regulates, and eventually exploits the seabed resources that underpin future industrial and military power. 
Rare earths may not define the South China Sea today, but they could help reshape how its strategic value is imagined tomorrow. 
In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.
The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.
Chen Wangwanyu is an assistant research fellow at Huayang Center for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance
articles.summary: The rise of seabed mining will add new complexity to the South China Sea disputes.
